Deep learning · chapter 2.3d · regularisation

Regularising Deep Networks

Penalties, noise, augmentation and sharing

A network with more weights than training examples can fit every point exactly, noise included, and then predict nonsense in between. Regularisation is any change to how we train that is meant to lower the error on new data, even if it raises the error on the training data. The tools look very different (a penalty on the weights, stopping early, jittering the inputs, softening the labels, forcing weights to be equal) but they all pull the same lever: they make the wiggly answers harder to reach. On the right are ten noisy points from a sine wave and a network with 12 hidden units. Pick a regulariser and turn the dial, or drag a point, and watch the wiggles go.

The goal
Lower test error, even at the price of some training error
Penalties

The problem

Too many weights, too little data

A network with one input, one output and M hidden units has 3M + 1 adjustable numbers. The number of hidden units sets how flexible it is, so the obvious way to control over-fitting is to choose M well: too few and the network cannot follow the curve, too many and it follows the noise. Bishop (PRML §5.5) shows the catch: the test error against M is a noisy cloud, because each training run starts from different random weights and lands in a different local minimum. Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman (ESL §11.5.2) put it bluntly: a network trained all the way to the global minimum of its training error will usually over-fit.

So in practice we take a network that is bigger than the data seem to justify and restrain it. Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville (Deep Learning ch. 7) define regularisation as any modification of the learning algorithm intended to reduce its generalisation error but not its training error. The simplest is to add a penalty on the size of the weights to the training error. Slide the number of hidden units and the penalty λ: the cloud on the right is the test error of eight training runs from different starting weights at each M.

\[ \begin{aligned} \widetilde{E}(\mathbf{w}) &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \big(y(x_n,\mathbf{w}) - t_n\big)^2 \\ &\quad + \frac{\lambda}{2}\,\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{w} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: y(xn, w) is the network’s output for input xn, tn the target, so the first term is the usual sum-of-squares training error. The second adds λ/2 times the sum of the squared weights. Training now balances fitting the points against keeping the weights small; λ = 0 is ordinary training. On this page the biases are left out of the penalty (you will see why in consistent priors).
Say it“E-tilde of w is a half the sum of squared errors plus lambda over two times w-transpose-w.”

test RMS error

Penalties · 1

Weight decay: a penalty and a prior

The penalty λ/2 ‖w‖² is called weight decay, and the name comes from what it does to a gradient step: before the usual step downhill, every weight is multiplied by a number slightly less than one, so a weight that the data do not keep pushing up decays towards zero. Russell and Norvig (AIMA §21.5.3) note that this is the same idea as ridge regression, and that it has a Bayesian reading: adding λ/2 ‖w‖² to the error is the same as finding the most probable weights under a Gaussian prior centred on zero (MAP estimation). Small weights also keep a tanh or sigmoid unit in its nearly linear middle, so a heavily decayed network behaves almost like a linear model.

Weight decay is not the only penalty. Hastie et al. describe weight elimination, which charges about λ for every weight that is clearly non-zero, however large, so it pushes small weights to zero while leaving the big ones alone. Switch between the penalties and slide λ, and watch both the curve and the 24 weights below it.

\[ \mathbf{w} \leftarrow (1-\eta\lambda)\,\mathbf{w} \;-\; \eta\,\nabla E(\mathbf{w}) \]
Read it as: the gradient of the penalised error is ∇E + λw, so one step of size η first shrinks every weight by the factor 1 − ηλ and then takes the ordinary step. (Adaptive optimisers such as Adam rescale the gradient per weight, which breaks this equivalence; “decoupled” weight decay, AdamW, applies the shrink directly instead.)
Say it“w becomes one minus eta lambda times w, minus eta times the gradient of E.”
\[ \begin{aligned} -\ln p(\mathbf{w}\mid\mathcal{D}) &= \frac{\beta}{2}\sum_n (y_n - t_n)^2 \\ &\quad + \frac{\alpha}{2}\,\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{w} + \text{const} \\ \lambda &= \alpha/\beta \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: if the targets are the network’s output plus Gaussian noise of precision β (variance 1/β), and the prior says each weight is Gaussian with mean 0 and precision α, then the negative log posterior is exactly the penalised error scaled by β. Its minimum is the MAP weight vector, and the penalty λ is the ratio of the two precisions.
Say it“Minus log posterior is beta over two times the squared errors plus alpha over two w-transpose-w; lambda is alpha over beta.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \Omega_{\text{elim}}(\mathbf{w}) &= \lambda \sum_i \frac{w_i^2}{1 + w_i^2} \\ \frac{\partial \Omega_{\text{elim}}}{\partial w_i} &= \frac{2\lambda\, w_i}{(1+w_i^2)^2} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: for a small weight, w²/(1 + w²) ≈ w², so it acts like weight decay; for a large weight it levels off at 1, so a big weight costs about λ no matter how big. The pull towards zero (the gradient) is strongest for weights of size about 0.58 and fades for large ones. ESL writes it with a scale w0; here w0 = 1.
Say it“Omega-elim is lambda times the sum of w-i squared over one plus w-i squared.”

Penalties · 2

Norm penalties as constrained optimisation

A penalty can be read as a budget. Suppose we insist that the weights stay inside a ball, Ω(w) ≤ k. The standard way to solve a constrained problem is a Lagrangian: add the constraint times a multiplier α ≥ 0 and look for a saddle point (Deep Learning §7.2). At the solution, α takes some value α*, and with α* fixed the problem is just the penalised one, J + α*Ω. So every penalty strength corresponds to a ball size and the other way round, although we rarely know which α goes with which k, because the match depends on the loss J.

Sometimes it is better to keep the constraint itself: take ordinary gradient steps and, whenever a step leaves the ball, project back to its surface (the nearest point inside). Two practical reasons are given in Deep Learning: a penalty keeps pulling weights towards zero even when that is unhelpful, which can leave units with tiny weights stuck, whereas a projection does nothing until the budget is exceeded; and a hard limit stops weights growing without bound when the learning rate is high. A common version caps the norm of each unit’s incoming weight vector (a max-norm constraint). Drag the unconstrained optimum w* and change the budget k; switch to the L1 ball to see why it produces exact zeros.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w},\alpha) &= J(\mathbf{w}) + \alpha\,\big(\Omega(\mathbf{w}) - k\big) \\ \widetilde{\mathbf{w}} &= \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \max_{\alpha \ge 0} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w},\alpha) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: J is the training loss, Ω the norm (here ½‖w‖² or ‖w‖₁), k the budget. If w breaks the budget, Ω − k > 0 and the inner maximisation would push α to infinity, so the outer minimisation must respect the budget. At the solution α* is a fixed number and w̃ minimises J + α*Ω: a penalised problem.
Say it“The Lagrangian is J of w plus alpha times omega of w minus k; w-tilde is the arg-min over w of the max over non-negative alpha.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \nabla J(\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}) + \alpha^{*}\,\nabla\Omega(\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}) &= \mathbf{0} \\ \text{L2: } \widetilde{w}_i &= \frac{h_i}{h_i + \alpha^{*}}\, w^{*}_i \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: at the constrained optimum the pull of the loss and the push of the constraint cancel (one of the KKT conditions; the other says α* = 0 if the budget is not binding). For a quadratic loss J = ½(w − w*)TH(w − w*), written in the eigen-directions of H with curvatures hi, the L2 solution shrinks each coordinate of w* by hi/(hi + α*): steep directions barely move, flat ones collapse.
Say it“Gradient of J plus alpha-star times gradient of omega is zero; for L2, each w-tilde-i is h-i over h-i plus alpha-star, times w-star-i.”

Penalties · 3

Consistent Gaussian priors

Here is a quiet flaw in plain weight decay (PRML §5.5.1). Suppose you measure the input in different units, x̃ = a x + b: centimetres instead of metres, say. A network trained on x̃ can represent exactly the same function as before: divide every first-layer weight by a and adjust the biases. Likewise if the targets are rescaled, t̃ = c t + d, multiply the second-layer weights by c. We would like the regulariser to be consistent: training on rescaled data should give the rescaled network, so the answer does not depend on the units you chose.

Plain weight decay fails this test: it treats all weights alike, so after the input is scaled by a, the first-layer weights that do the same job are a times smaller and the penalty on them shrinks by a². The fix is one penalty per layer, with the biases left out, and strengths that are rescaled with the data. In the language of priors, each group of weights gets its own precision αk. Such a prior is improper (the unpenalised biases have a flat distribution that cannot be normalised), which matters only if you want to compare models by their evidence; then the biases need priors of their own. Taking one group per input gives automatic relevance determination, where an input whose weights get a huge α is effectively switched off. Change the input’s units with the slider and compare plain decay with the consistent version.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\widetilde{x} = a x + b: \\ &\quad \widetilde{w}_{ji} = \tfrac{1}{a} w_{ji} \\ &\quad \widetilde{w}_{j0} = w_{j0} - \tfrac{b}{a}\textstyle\sum_i w_{ji} \\ &\widetilde{t} = c\, t + d: \\ &\quad \widetilde{w}_{kj} = c\, w_{kj}, \;\; \widetilde{w}_{k0} = c\, w_{k0} + d \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: wji are the first-layer weights (input i to hidden unit j), wj0 their biases; wkj and wk0 are the second layer’s. Each new network computes exactly the old function in the new units: the hidden units see the same inputs (a x·w/a = x w), and the output is stretched and shifted like the targets.
Say it“Scaling the input by a divides the first-layer weights by a; scaling the targets by c multiplies the second-layer weights by c.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \frac{\lambda_1}{2}\!\sum_{w \in \mathcal{W}_1}\! w^2 \\ &\quad + \frac{\lambda_2}{2}\!\sum_{w \in \mathcal{W}_2}\! w^2 \\ \lambda_1 &\to a^2 \lambda_1, \quad \lambda_2 \to \lambda_2 / c^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: W1 holds the first-layer weights, W2 the second-layer weights; biases are in neither. Under the rescaling the first sum shrinks by a² and the second grows by c², so rescaling λ1 and λ2 as shown leaves Ω unchanged for equivalent networks. (Bishop’s printed exponents differ; squaring follows directly from w → w/a.)
Say it“Omega is lambda-one over two times the first-layer squares plus lambda-two over two times the second-layer squares; lambda-one becomes a squared lambda-one.”
\[ \begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{w}\mid\boldsymbol{\alpha}) &\propto \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\alpha_1}{2}\!\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}_1}\! w^2\Big) \\ &\quad \times \exp\!\Big(- \frac{\alpha_2}{2}\!\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}_2}\! w^2\Big) \\ p(\mathbf{w}) &\propto \exp\!\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_k \alpha_k \lVert \mathbf{w}\rVert_k^2\Big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the matching prior gives each layer its own precision α1, α2 (the λs up to the noise precision β). The right-hand form generalises to any partition of the weights into groups k, with ‖w‖k² the sum of squares in group k.
Say it“The prior is proportional to e to the minus alpha-one over two times the first-layer squares minus alpha-two over two times the second-layer squares.”
largest gap between the two fits
λ₁ used on x̃

To isolate the penalty, the optimiser is made unit-free too: plain gradient descent whose step for first-layer weights is divided by a². With λ = 0 the two fits would then agree exactly for every a.

Regularising by time

Early stopping

Watch a network train and the error on the training set falls steadily, while the error on a separate validation set usually falls, flattens and then rises as the network starts fitting noise. Early stopping keeps the weights from the iteration with the lowest validation error (PRML §5.5.2, Deep Learning §7.8, ESL §11.5.2). In practice you save a copy whenever the validation error improves, and give up after it has failed to improve for a set number of checks (the patience). It costs almost nothing, needs no change to the model or the loss, and the number of steps becomes a hyperparameter tuned in a single run. Its price is the data held back for validation; afterwards you can either retrain on all the data for the same number of steps, or continue training on all the data until the training loss falls to the value it had at the stopping point.

Why does stopping early regularise? Training starts from small weights and moves outward, so stopping early keeps the weights small, like weight decay. For a quadratic loss the link is exact enough to write down. Move the stopping point in the first lab, then compare the two paths in the second.

\[ \tau^{*} = \arg\min_{\tau}\; E_{\text{val}}\big(\mathbf{w}^{(\tau)}\big) \]
Read it as: w(τ) is the weight vector after τ training steps; Eval is the error on data not used for training. Keep the weights at the step where the validation error is lowest. The effective complexity of the network (Bishop calls it the effective number of parameters) grows as training goes on.
Say it“Tau-star is the arg-min over tau of the validation error of w after tau steps.”
training RMS
validation RMS
test RMS (200 points)
‖w‖

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{GD:}\;\; w^{(\tau)}_i &= \big[1 - (1-\varepsilon h_i)^{\tau}\big]\, w^{*}_i \\ \text{L2:}\;\; \widetilde{w}_i &= \Big[1 - \frac{\alpha}{h_i + \alpha}\Big]\, w^{*}_i \\ \text{match:}\;\; \alpha &\approx \frac{1}{\tau\varepsilon} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: for a quadratic loss with curvatures hi (eigenvalues of the Hessian) and step size ϵ, each coordinate of w* (in the eigen-directions) is reached at its own pace: steep directions in a few steps, flat ones slowly. Weight decay with strength α shrinks the same coordinates by a similar factor. When ϵhi is small and hi is small next to α (directions the training has barely moved along), taking logarithms of the two shrink factors makes them equal for α = 1/(τϵ): the number of steps plays the role of an inverse penalty.
Say it“After tau steps, w-i is one minus one-minus-epsilon-h-i to the tau, times w-star-i; this matches weight decay with alpha about one over tau epsilon.”
matching α = 1/(τϵ)

Regularising with data

Dataset augmentation and transformed data

The best regulariser is more data. When you cannot collect it, you can often manufacture it: if you know a change to the input should not change the answer, apply it to the training examples and keep their labels (Deep Learning §7.4). For photographs, shifting by a few pixels, mirroring left to right, small rotations and changes of scale, brightness and contrast are the standard moves (§12.2.1.2); cutting out a random square forces the network not to rely on one patch. Augmentation is a form of prior knowledge, and it can be wrong: mirroring a “b” makes a “d”, rotating a “6” by 180° makes a “9”, and an upside-down cat is not what the camera will see. Augmentation is applied to the training data only; when you compare two methods, compare them with the same augmentation.

Bishop (PRML §5.5.3) lists four ways to make a model invariant to a transformation: (1) augment the training set with transformed copies; (2) add a penalty for changing the output when the input is transformed (tangent propagation, next chapter); (3) pre-process the inputs into features that are already invariant; (4) build the invariance into the network, as convolution does (below). Turn transformations on and off and draw new samples from the real photographs used in the project.

\[ \begin{aligned} \widetilde{E}(\mathbf{w}) &= \sum_{n=1}^{N} \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\xi}\sim p(\boldsymbol{\xi})}\big[\, \ell_n(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \big] \\ \ell_n(\boldsymbol{\xi}) &= \ell\big(f(s(\mathbf{x}_n,\boldsymbol{\xi});\mathbf{w}),\, t_n\big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: s(x, ξ) transforms the input x by an amount ξ (a shift, an angle, a flip…) drawn at random from p(ξ); ℓ is the loss. Training on augmented data minimises the average loss over all those transformed copies, and in practice each minibatch draws a fresh ξ for every image, so the network rarely sees exactly the same picture twice.
Say it“E-tilde is the sum over examples of the expected loss on the transformed input s of x-n and xi.”
Transformations
distinct views in the project
mean pixel change

For small transformations there is a precise statement of what augmentation does (PRML §5.5.5). Expand the loss on a transformed input as a Taylor series in the size of the transformation ξ. Averaging over ξ adds terms in its variance, and to leading order (Bishop shows the remaining term vanishes at the optimum) training on transformed data is the same as training on the original data with an extra penalty: the squared rate at which the output changes along the transformation. When the transformation is random noise added to the inputs, that penalty is the squared gradient of the output, ‖∇y‖², the classical Tikhonov regulariser (Bishop, 1995). The second lab checks this on a model that is linear in its weights (a bias and 9 Gaussian bumps), so both versions can be solved exactly. Raise the noise σ and see whether 50 noisy copies of each point give the same curve as the penalty.

\[ \begin{aligned} \widetilde{E} &= E + \sigma^2\, \Omega + O(\sigma^4) \\ \Omega &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{n} \big(\boldsymbol{\tau}_n^{\mathsf T}\nabla y(\mathbf{x}_n)\big)^2 \\ \text{noise:}\;\; \Omega &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_n \big\lVert \nabla y(\mathbf{x}_n) \big\rVert^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: E is the sum-of-squares error, σ² the variance of the transformation amount, τn the direction in which the transformation moves xn (its tangent vector). The penalty is large when the output changes quickly as the input is transformed. For additive Gaussian noise every direction counts equally, giving the squared gradient. In one dimension: Ω = ½Σ y′(xn)².
Say it“E-tilde equals E plus sigma squared omega; omega is a half the sum of the squared slopes of y along the transformation.”
largest gap: copies vs penalty
test RMS, plain fit
test RMS, noisy copies

Regularising with noise

Noise robustness and label smoothing

Noise can be injected in three places (Deep Learning §7.5). On the inputs it is augmentation, and for small noise a penalty on the slope, as you just saw. On the hidden units it leads to dropout (the next chapter). On the weights it says: a good solution should still be good if the weights are jostled. For regression, adding small Gaussian noise of variance η to the weights adds roughly η times the squared sensitivity of the output to the weights, which steers training towards wide, flat valleys of the loss rather than narrow ones. Raise the weight noise in the first lab and watch which minimum wins.

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\big[ L(\mathbf{w}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \big] &\approx L(\mathbf{w}) \\ &\quad + \frac{s^2}{2}\,\operatorname{tr} \nabla^2 L(\mathbf{w}) \\ \boldsymbol{\epsilon} &\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, s^2 I) \\ \mathbb{E}\big[(\hat y_{\boldsymbol\epsilon} - y)^2\big] &\approx \mathbb{E}\big[(\hat y - y)^2\big] \\ &\quad + s^2\, \mathbb{E}\big[\lVert \nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\, \hat y \rVert^2\big] \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: averaged over random jolts of size s, the loss is the loss plus s²/2 times its total curvature (the trace of the Hessian): sharp minima are taxed, flat ones are not. For squared error, the dominant part of that tax is the squared gradient of the prediction with respect to the weights (with s² playing the role of η).
Say it“The expected loss under weight noise is about the loss plus s squared over two times the trace of the Hessian.”
best w under noise
expected loss, sharp valley
expected loss, flat valley

Noise can also go on the outputs. Labels are sometimes wrong, and a classifier trained with hard 0/1 targets and a softmax can never reach its target: the probability of the right class only approaches 1 as its logit runs away to infinity, so on separable data the weights keep growing (weight decay is one way to stop that). Label smoothing (Deep Learning §7.5.1) replaces the hard targets with 1 − ε for the labelled class and ε/(K − 1) for each of the others. The cross-entropy then has a finite minimum: the model is rewarded for being confident, but not certain. (Szegedy et al., 2016, popularised a variant that mixes in the uniform distribution, giving 1 − ε + ε/K to the labelled class.) Move ε and the number of classes K.

\[ \begin{aligned} q_k &= \begin{cases} 1-\varepsilon & k = y \\ \varepsilon/(K-1) & k \ne y \end{cases} \\ L &= -\sum_{k=1}^{K} q_k \ln p_k \\ \Delta^{*} &= \ln\frac{(1-\varepsilon)(K-1)}{\varepsilon} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: y is the labelled class, pk the softmax probabilities, qk the smoothed targets. If the K − 1 wrong classes share the same logit and the right class is Δ above them, then py = eΔ/(eΔ + K − 1). The loss is lowest when p matches q exactly, which happens at the gap Δ*: beyond it, extra confidence is penalised. With ε = 0 there is no minimum, and Δ drifts to infinity.
Say it“The target is one minus epsilon for the true class and epsilon over K minus one for the rest; the best logit gap is the log of one-minus-epsilon times K-minus-one over epsilon.”
best logit gap Δ*
highest confidence rewarded
lowest possible loss

Regularising with structure

Invariances, parameter tying and parameter sharing

Penalties pull weights towards zero, but often we know something sharper: that two weights should be similar. If two models solve related tasks, parameter tying adds a penalty on the distance between their weights (Deep Learning §7.9). Push that penalty to infinity and the weights become identical: parameter sharing. Sharing is the most effective regulariser in deep learning, because it builds an invariance into the network (Bishop’s fourth route) and divides the number of free parameters, and the memory to store them, by the number of places they are reused. A convolutional layer is exactly this: the same small filter, slid across every position of the image.

The lab makes that concrete. Each sequence of 16 numbers is noise, and the positive ones also contain a short pattern (a motif, here +1, −1, +1). The detector has a separate 3-tap filter for each of the 14 positions where the motif can start, and pools their scores. But the training motifs only ever appear in the first half of the sequence. Untied, the filters for the second half never see a motif. Tied, they are pulled towards the filters that did. Increase the tying strength β, or share outright, and test on motifs at every position.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{A, B:}\;\; \Omega_{\text{tie}} &= \lVert \mathbf{w}^{(A)} - \mathbf{w}^{(B)} \rVert_2^2 \\ \text{filters:}\;\; \Omega_{\text{tie}} &= \frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{p=1}^{P} \lVert \mathbf{k}_p - \bar{\mathbf{k}} \rVert^2 \\ \bar{\mathbf{k}} &= \frac{1}{P}\sum_{p} \mathbf{k}_p \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: the left form ties two models A and B. The right form ties P filters kp, one per position, by penalising each one’s distance from their average k̄. With β = 0 they are independent; as β → ∞ all filters equal k̄, which is a convolution with a single shared filter and P times fewer parameters.
Say it“Omega-tie is beta over two times the sum over positions of the squared distance between k-p and the mean filter k-bar.”
free parameters
detected, positions 1–7
detected, positions 8–14

Regularising with structure · 2

Soft weight sharing

Hard sharing needs you to decide in advance which weights are equal. Soft weight sharing (Nowlan and Hinton, 1992; PRML §5.5.7) lets the data decide. The prior on each weight is a mixture of a few Gaussians, and the mixture is learned along with the weights: weights that sit near the same centre are pulled together, so the network ends up with a handful of distinct values instead of many unrelated ones. Weight decay is the special case of one component, fixed at zero.

The lab uses a model where this is easy to see: a linear regression with 20 weights fitted to 30 noisy examples. The data were simulated so that the true weights take only three values (−1, 0 and 1.5), but the model is not told that. Ordinary least squares scatters the estimates; weight decay drags them all towards zero; a three-component mixture finds the groups. Press Run and watch the weights (dots) and the mixture (curve) organise each other.

\[ \begin{aligned} \widetilde{E} &= E(\mathbf{w}) + \lambda\,\Omega(\mathbf{w}) \\ \Omega &= -\sum_{i} \ln\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{M} \pi_j \mathcal{N}(w_i \mid \mu_j, \sigma_j^2)\Big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: Ω is the negative log of a mixture prior, evaluated at every weight wi; the components have mixing weights πj, centres μj and widths σj, all learned. A weight close to some centre costs little. Here E is half the sum of squared errors (noise variance 1), so λ = 1 is the exact Bayesian weighting.
Say it“Omega is minus the sum over weights of the log of the mixture density at that weight.”
\[ \begin{aligned} \gamma_j(w) &= \frac{\pi_j \mathcal{N}(w\mid\mu_j,\sigma_j^2)}{\sum_k \pi_k \mathcal{N}(w\mid\mu_k,\sigma_k^2)} \\ \frac{\partial \widetilde{E}}{\partial w_i} &= \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_i} + \lambda \sum_j \gamma_j(w_i)\tfrac{w_i - \mu_j}{\sigma_j^2} \\ \frac{\partial \widetilde{E}}{\partial \mu_j} &= \lambda \sum_i \gamma_j(w_i)\tfrac{\mu_j - w_i}{\sigma_j^2} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: γj(w) is the responsibility of component j for a weight w, as in a Gaussian mixture. Each weight is pulled towards the centres in proportion to their responsibility; each centre moves towards the weights it is responsible for. The widths and mixing weights have similar gradients; the mixing weights are written as a softmax πj = eηj/Σkeηk, whose gradient is λΣi(πj − γj(wi)).
Say it“Each weight is pulled toward each centre by its responsibility times the distance over the variance.”

Real-world project

Project: cat or dog, from 1,000 photographs

The Oxford-IIIT Pet Dataset (Parkhi, Vedaldi, Zisserman and Jawahar, 2012) has 7,349 photographs of 37 breeds of cats and dogs, released under CC BY-SA 4.0. For most of the “trainval” photographs the authors also drew a box around the animal’s head. This project uses those boxes: each head is cut out (the box squared up with a 15% margin), turned to grey and shrunk to 28 × 28 pixels with 16 grey levels, small enough for the whole set to travel inside this page. From the 3,671 boxed photographs, a seeded random draw picked 950 cats and 950 dogs: 1,000 for training (500 of each), 300 for validation and 600 for testing. The task: cat or dog?

The network is a small convolutional net: a 5 × 5 convolution with 8 filters, ReLU and 2 × 2 max-pooling, then a 3 × 3 convolution with 16 filters, ReLU and pooling, then a dense layer to two outputs: 1,890 parameters, which already share their weights across positions. It sees a 24 × 24 window. It is trained by minibatch SGD (batch 32, step 0.05) for 30 epochs, in eight versions: with or without augmentation (a random shift of up to 2 pixels each way and a random left–right mirror, drawn afresh for every image in every epoch), weight decay (λ = 0.01 on the convolution and dense weights, not the biases) and label smoothing (ε = 0.1). Every version starts from the same initial weights, and the minibatch order and the augmentations come from one seeded random generator. Early stopping is read off each run: the epoch with the lowest validation loss.

2 · Eight training runs

First-layer filters (5 × 5)

The same experiment in Python

import sys, json, numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0, ".")                    # python -I does not add the script folder
import x053_ref as R                       # numpy version of the page's network (im2col convolutions)
d = np.load("x053_dl/pets.npz")            # 1,900 head crops, 28 x 28, grey levels 0..15; label 0 = cat, 1 = dog
q, y, ntr, nva = d["q"], d["y"], int(d["ntr"]), int(d["nva"])
A = R.Arch(S=24, k1=5, C1=8, C2=16)        # conv 5x5x8, pool, conv 3x3x16, pool, dense 256 -> 2
base = dict(seed=7, train=list(range(ntr)), val=list(range(ntr, ntr + nva)), test=list(range(ntr + nva, len(y))),
            batch=32, lr=0.05, epochs=30, pad=2)            # step size falls linearly from 0.05 towards 0
print(f"train {ntr} (dogs {y[:ntr].sum()}), validation {nva}, test {len(y) - ntr - nva}; "
      f"parameters {sum(p.size for p in R.init(A, 7))}")
out = {}
for aug in (0, 1):
    for wd in (0.0, 0.01):
        for ls in (0.0, 0.1):
            h, P = R.train(A, q, 28, y, dict(base, aug=bool(aug), wd=wd, ls=ls), epochs=30)
            b = min(h, key=lambda r: r["vaLoss"])          # early stopping: lowest validation loss
            print(f"aug {aug} wd {wd:<4} ls {ls:<3} | train {h[-1]['trAcc']:.3f} test {h[-1]['teAcc']:.4f} "
                  f"NLL {h[-1]['teLoss']:.4f} |w| {h[-1]['wnorm']:.3f} | early stop: epoch {b['epoch']:2d} test {b['teAcc']:.4f}")
            X = np.stack([R.load(q, 28, n, A.S, 0, 0, False) for n in base["test"]]); z, _ = R.forward(A, P, X)
            pdog = 1 / (1 + np.exp(z[:, 0] - z[:, 1]))
            out[f"{aug}{int(wd > 0)}{int(ls > 0)}"] = dict(h=h, p=[int(v) for v in np.floor(pdog * 100).clip(0, 99)],
                                                           k1=[round(float(v), 4) for v in P[0].ravel()])
first = out["000"]["h"][0]
print("epoch 1, no regulariser:", " ".join(f"{k} {v:.12f}" for k, v in first.items() if k != "epoch"))
json.dump(out, open("x053-ref.json", "w"))

The browser’s network is a separate JavaScript implementation (plain loops over typed arrays) of the same maths as the numpy reference (vectorised im2col). Both draw the initial weights, the minibatch order and every augmentation from the same seeded generator (mulberry32), so they should agree to rounding; the live run above reports the largest difference it finds. Honest caveats: this is one seed and one split, so differences of a few points are noise; the images are tiny (28 × 28, 16 grey levels) and the network is small, so the accuracies are far below what a modern pretrained network reaches on full-size photographs; and the regularisation strengths were set once by hand, not tuned.

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • Regularisation is anything that aims to lower test error rather than training error; in practice we use a network that is too big and restrain it.
  • Weight decay adds λ/2 ‖w‖²: it shrinks every weight a little each step, equals MAP estimation under a Gaussian prior, and corresponds to a norm budget through a Lagrange multiplier. Give each layer its own λ and leave the biases out, so the answer does not depend on units.
  • Early stopping keeps the weights with the lowest validation error; for a quadratic loss, τ steps of size ϵ act like weight decay with α ≈ 1/(τϵ).
  • Augmentation trains on label-preserving transformations of the data; for small transformations it equals a penalty on how fast the output changes along them (Tikhonov for input noise). Noise on weights favours flat minima; label smoothing caps the confidence a softmax is pushed towards.
  • Tying pulls weights towards each other; sharing makes them equal and builds in invariance, as convolution does; soft weight sharing learns the groups with a mixture prior.

Check your understanding

With learning rate η = 0.1 and λ = 0.001, what does weight decay do to a weight in one step if its loss gradient is zero?

It multiplies the weight by 1 − ηλ = 1 − 0.0001 = 0.9999. Over 10,000 such steps that compounds to about e−1 ≈ 0.37, so weights the data do not support fade away slowly.

Why are the biases usually left out of the weight-decay penalty?

A bias only shifts a unit’s input; it does not make the function more wiggly, and under a change of units the biases must absorb shifts (b̃ = b − (b/a)Σw). Penalising them would make the fit depend on where you put the zero of each variable, which is exactly the inconsistency the per-layer prior avoids. The cost is an improper prior.

Your validation loss is lowest at epoch 12, but you trained for 30. What do you ship, and how could you use the validation data afterwards?

The weights saved at epoch 12. Then either retrain from scratch on training plus validation data for the same number of steps (about 12 epochs’ worth of updates), or continue training the epoch-12 model on all the data until its training loss falls to the validation loss it had at the stopping point.

Would you mirror images left to right when training a digit recogniser? A pet classifier?

Not for digits or letters: a mirrored 2 or b is a different symbol, so the transformation changes the label. For pets, yes: a cat facing left is still a cat. Upside-down flips are a bad idea for both, because they never occur in the test data.

With label smoothing ε = 0.1 and K = 2 classes, what is the most confident prediction the loss rewards, and what logit gap gives it?

The target for the labelled class is 0.9, so the loss is lowest at p = 0.9, which needs a gap Δ* = ln(0.9 × 1/0.1) = ln 9 ≈ 2.20. Any larger gap raises the loss.
